title: Affordable housing strategy and housing pledge approved
subtitle: Also: road reconstruction tenders, festival policy, strategic plan workshop, lot maintenance and Reep Green Solutions presentations.
overview: Council approved the 2023-2033 Affordable Housing Strategy and a Municipal Housing Pledge to the Province of planning for 16,000 residential units by 2031. The strategy sets out actions to help low and moderate income households. Staff will start the actions that fit existing work plans and will begin budgeting for the rest, including a possible Affordable Housing Policy Planner, through the 2024-2026 budget process {{vote:m5}}. The pledge will be reported on each year, and Council urged the Province to give municipalities more money to offset the effects of Bill 23 {{vote:m6}}.

Council also approved a significant package of road and infrastructure spending: $1.3 million moved to the King Street reconstruction {{vote:m7}}, $7,307,000 for the 2023 city-wide road improvement program plus $300,000 for Columbia Street {{vote:m8}}, and three tender awards for road reconstruction and annual paving {{vote:m9}} {{vote:m10}} {{vote:m11}}. Council also approved an updated policy on significant festivals and events {{vote:m3}}.

Delegations spoke on the lot maintenance by-law and naturalized yards, and Reep Green Solutions presented its impact report. Council also held its third strategic plan workshop on vision and guiding principles. The draft plan is due May 8 and the final plan June 26.

decisions.detail: Council approved the strategy, directed staff to advance actions needing no new resources, and to begin budgeting for the mid- to longer-term actions, including considering an Affordable Housing Policy Planner, in the 2024-2026 budget process.

Council approved submitting a pledge to plan for 16,000 residential units by 2031, directed annual reporting, and urged the Province to provide more financial help to municipalities affected by Bill 23.
Council authorized moving $1,300,000 in capital funding from various capital project accounts to the King Street Reconstruction project.
Council approved $300,000 for Columbia Street and $7,307,000 for the 2023 city-wide road improvement program.

decisions.item: Annual asphalt paving and concrete repairs tender
decisions.detail: Council awarded the two-year tender to Sousa Concrete for a total of $7,767,704.08 including unrecoverable HST.

decisions.item: Teakwood Dr., Teakwood Pl. and Thorncrest Dr. reconstruction
decisions.detail: Council awarded the road reconstruction tender to T. Musselman Excavating Limited for a total of $2,987,371.29 including unrecoverable HST.
Council awarded the road reconstruction tender to Steed and Evans Limited for a total of $1,365,619.20 including unrecoverable HST.
Council approved the amended policy and the 2023 list of designated festivals and events, which receive blanket by-law exemptions.

debate: A delegate on the lot maintenance by-law argued that rules on grass height, buffer strips and "unkempt" appearance discourage naturalized yards that support insects, birds and pollinators, and urged complaint-based enforcement focused on actual harm. Staff said the by-law was amended last year to permit naturalized areas, that buffer strips and height limits reflect sight-line and safety feedback, and that Transportation is preparing a report on boulevard plantings.

On the Affordable Housing Strategy, a councillor worried that actions would be handled "off the side of the desk" without a dedicated policy planner. Staff said the main risk is a slower pace of implementation, and another councillor backed having one person coordinate the work.

Delegates supported the strategy but urged going further. They asked for more missing-middle housing across the whole city rather than only in nodes and corridors, leasing rather than selling city land, and stronger protections for existing rental housing. Staff said leasing city land would be considered, and explained that a blanket four-units, four-storeys rule raised concerns about parking, landscaping and transit access.

On the housing pledge, councillors noted the city does not build homes itself and asked how much of the target the city can control. Staff said annual reporting would allow check-ins and that the city has visibility on about 20,000 units. Several councillors said the Province should provide more funding and address development industry constraints.

A councillor asked that future versions of the festivals policy address sustainability. Staff said this policy is administrative, offered to develop sustainability toolkits for the volunteer-run festivals, and said the Business Improvement Area can seek by-law exemptions event by event.
